report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy for Existential Distress in Serious and Life-Limiting Illness: Emerging Trial Evidence, Barriers to Access, and the Case for Individualized Eligibility

author.affiliation:

								Medrego Ltd

									Latvia

text.text: Background.
Existential distress and treatment-resistant depression are common and difficult to manage in patients with serious and life-limiting illnesses.
Psilocybin-assisted therapy has shown early promise for these conditions, but access outside research settings remains narrow, inconsistent, expensive and often shaped by outdated eligibility rules.
These include narrow lists of qualifying diagnoses and blanket age-based cut-offs that are not grounded in evidence specific to palliative populations.
Regulators slowly adjust to the state-of-the-art knowledge generated by psilocybin-assisted therapy, and overall, often show poor understanding of palliative populations' specific needs.
Objective.

To review current and emerging clinical evidence for psilocybin-assisted therapy in serious and life-limiting illness, highlighted with the examples of the EU "Horizon Europe" funded PsyPal project and a Johns Hopkins-led trial in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and to examine the regulatory, informational, and financial barriers that shape access for palliative populations.
Findings.
Randomized trials in cancer-related existential distress report sustained reductions in depression and death anxiety.
Furthermore, a majority of participants in the founding psilocybin studies rated their session among the most meaningful experiences of their life.

Project PsyPal is currently the first randomized trial of psilocybin therapy in non-oncology palliative populations, enrolling patients with COPD, ALS, multiple sclerosis, and atypical parkinsonian disorders across four European sites with no upper age limit; a separate trial at Johns Hopkins is testing psilocybin for mood and hopelessness in ALS specifically.
Real-world cohort data from Oregon's regulated program corroborate meaningful symptom improvement and low serious-adverse-event rates.

Access, however, remains constrained by diagnostic and research-representation gaps, high outof-pocket cost, and inconsistent regulatory pathways, illustrated by a Canadian patient refused psilocybin for existential relief who was approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks.
Two U.S. psilocybin new drug applications, for treatment-resistant and for major depression, were completed in November 2026, but neither addresses existential distress.
Clinical evidence relevant to palliative and serious-illness populations is accumulating rapidly.

Eligibility frameworks for psilocybin-assisted therapy in palliative care should be built on individualized clinical assessment rather than systematic exclusions, paired with funding mechanisms that prevent access from becoming a function of wealth alone.

Existential distress -the anguish that accompanies an awareness of approaching death, loss of meaning, or loss of self -is among the most difficult symptoms palliative care clinicians are asked to treat.

Standard pharmacological approaches to depression and anxiety in this context are frequently slow to act, poorly tolerated in patients with advanced disease, or simply insufficient for suffering that is existential rather than purely biochemical in origin 1 .
text.formatted: Standard pharmacological approaches to depression and anxiety in this context are frequently slow to act, poorly tolerated in patients with advanced disease, or simply insufficient for suffering that is existential rather than purely biochemical in origin <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">1</ref> .

text.text: Against this gap, psilocybin-assisted therapy has re-emerged over the past two decades as a candidate intervention, supported by early but consistent signals in patients with cancer-related distress 2, 3.
text.formatted: Against this gap, psilocybin-assisted therapy has re-emerged over the past two decades as a candidate intervention, supported by early but consistent signals in patients with cancer-related distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">3</ref>.

text.text: Interest has grown quickly, but the evidence base specific to palliative and serious-illness populations outside oncology has, until recently, been almost nonexistent.

Most of what is known about psilocybin's safety and effect comes from trials in physically healthy or psychiatric populations, not from patients living with COPD, ALS, multiple sclerosis, or atypical parkinsonian disorders, nor reliably from the oldest patients within any diagnosis, who are systematically underrepresented in psychedelic trials generally 4, 5 .
text.formatted: Most of what is known about psilocybin's safety and effect comes from trials in physically healthy or psychiatric populations, not from patients living with COPD, ALS, multiple sclerosis, or atypical parkinsonian disorders, nor reliably from the oldest patients within any diagnosis, who are systematically underrepresented in psychedelic trials generally <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">5</ref> .

text.text: This article reviews the evidence now closing that gap, with particular attention to two current trial programs -the European Union "Horizon Europe" funded PsyPal consortium and a Johns Hopkins-led trial in ALS -that are, between them, the first sustained effort to generate palliative-population-specific data for psilocybin therapy.
Evidence alone, however, does not determine access.

This article therefore also examines the regulatory, informational, and financial barriers that shape whether a patient who might benefit from psilocybin-assisted therapy can actually obtain it, and argues that eligibility should rest on individualized clinical assessment -capacity, relevant risk factors, and informed consentrather than on systematic exclusions, including the age-based cut-offs still common in trial design and some regulatory frameworks, that are not well adjusted to the evidence reviewed here.
Section 2 reviews the trial evidence and Section 3 examines access barriers relevant to palliative care systems.
Section 4 sets out the ethical case for individualized eligibility.
Section 5 reviews international regulatory approaches, and Section 6 translates these findings into policy and practice recommendations.

Sources for this review were identified through targeted searches of PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and medRxiv for psilocybin trials and cohort studies in palliative, oncology, and serious-illness populations published or registered through November 2026, supplemented by institutional and consortium communications for trials not yet reporting peer-reviewed results (PsyPal, the Johns Hopkins ALS trial).
It is not a systematic review, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed; evidence levels for each source are indicated in Table 1.
text.formatted: It is not a systematic review, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed; evidence levels for each source are indicated in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: The clearest existing evidence for psilocybin-assisted therapy in serious illness comes from oncology.

Two randomized, placebo-controlled trials found that a single moderate-to-high dose of psilocybin, combined with psychological support, produced substantial reductions in depression and death-related anxiety in patients with life-threatening cancer, sustained at six months in roughly 60-80% of participants 2, 3 .
text.formatted: Two randomized, placebo-controlled trials found that a single moderate-to-high dose of psilocybin, combined with psychological support, produced substantial reductions in depression and death-related anxiety in patients with life-threatening cancer, sustained at six months in roughly 60-80% of participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">3</ref> .

text.text: A more recent, uncontrolled follow-up of a similar protocol found that about half of participants sustained a significant reduction in depressive symptoms at two years, the longest follow-up reported for this population to date 6 .
text.formatted: A more recent, uncontrolled follow-up of a similar protocol found that about half of participants sustained a significant reduction in depressive symptoms at two years, the longest follow-up reported for this population to date <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">6</ref> .

text.text: In the founding Johns Hopkins study of psilocybin in healthy volunteers, 67% of participants rated their session as the single most meaningful experience of their life or among the top five, comparable in magnitude to the birth of a first child, with ratings holding at 14-month follow-up 7, 8 .
text.formatted: In the founding Johns Hopkins study of psilocybin in healthy volunteers, 67% of participants rated their session as the single most meaningful experience of their life or among the top five, comparable in magnitude to the birth of a first child, with ratings holding at 14-month follow-up <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8</ref> .

text.text: Part of what makes the experience significant may be relational rather than purely symptomatic: a randomized, placebocontrolled trial in patients with major depression found that a single dose of psilocybin produced a measurable increase in emotional empathy still detectable two weeks later 9 , a dimension that may matter as much to a patient with a life-limiting illness and a lifetime of relationships behind them as any depression or anxiety score.
text.formatted: Part of what makes the experience significant may be relational rather than purely symptomatic: a randomized, placebocontrolled trial in patients with major depression found that a single dose of psilocybin produced a measurable increase in emotional empathy still detectable two weeks later <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9</ref> , a dimension that may matter as much to a patient with a life-limiting illness and a lifetime of relationships behind them as any depression or anxiety score.

text.text: This personal-meaning finding is consistent with the geriatric psychiatrist Robert Butler's description of the "life review," a naturally occurring process of looking back over one's life that contributes to serenity when it resolves well and to late-life depression when it stalls 10.
text.formatted: This personal-meaning finding is consistent with the geriatric psychiatrist Robert Butler's description of the "life review," a naturally occurring process of looking back over one's life that contributes to serenity when it resolves well and to late-life depression when it stalls <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">10</ref>.

text.text: A November 2026 integrative systematic review of psilocybin-assisted therapy for cancer-related psychological and existential distress reached a consistent conclusion, describing the intervention as promising but still investigational 11 .
text.formatted: A November 2026 integrative systematic review of psilocybin-assisted therapy for cancer-related psychological and existential distress reached a consistent conclusion, describing the intervention as promising but still investigational <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11</ref> .

text.text: These findings, while robust for their design, come from a single diagnostic population.

Whether they generalize to the range of conditions palliative care actually manages -progressive neurological and respiratory disease, multi-morbidity, cognitive change -has, until recently, been untested.

The PsyPal consortium, funded under "Horizon Europe", the EU Framework Programme for Research and Innovation, is conducting the first randomized trial to examine psilocybin therapy specifically in non-oncology palliative populations 12 .
text.formatted: The PsyPal consortium, funded under "Horizon Europe", the EU Framework Programme for Research and Innovation, is conducting the first randomized trial to examine psilocybin therapy specifically in non-oncology palliative populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12</ref> .

text.text: Led by Prof.

Robert Schoevers at the University Medical Center Groningen, this randomized, double-blind, low-dose-controlled Phase 2 trial is enrolling an estimated 108 participants with one of four progressive, life-limiting conditions across four European clinical sites: COPD at the University Medical Center Groningen in the Netherlands, atypical parkinsonian disorders at the Champalimaud Foundation in Portugal, multiple sclerosis at the National Institute of Mental Health in the Czech Republic, and ALS jointly at the University of Copenhagen and Bispebjerg Hospital in Denmark 13 .
text.formatted: Robert Schoevers at the University Medical Center Groningen, this randomized, double-blind, low-dose-controlled Phase 2 trial is enrolling an estimated 108 participants with one of four progressive, life-limiting conditions across four European clinical sites: COPD at the University Medical Center Groningen in the Netherlands, atypical parkinsonian disorders at the Champalimaud Foundation in Portugal, multiple sclerosis at the National Institute of Mental Health in the Czech Republic, and ALS jointly at the University of Copenhagen and Bispebjerg Hospital in Denmark <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13</ref> .

text.text: Participants attend three preparation sessions with psychotherapists (1-2 hours each), two supervised dosing sessions (6-8 hours each) given two weeks apart, and five integration sessions.
The experimental group receives two escalating doses of psilocybin (15 mg, then 25 mg); the control group receives two low doses (1 mg).

Follow-up assessments take place at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months, with access to a digital care platform and peer support groups throughout follow-up, and control-group participants may receive one open-label 25 mg session after the primary endpoint.
The trial sets no upper age limit for enrollment 12 .
text.formatted: The trial sets no upper age limit for enrollment <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12</ref> .

text.text: Its primary purpose is classified as supportive care; the primary endpoint is change in depression severity (MADRS) from baseline to 6 weeks after the second dosing session, and secondary outcomes include anxiety, demoralization, quality of life, and longer-term patient and family wellbeing, an endpoint the investigators have specifically noted is often overlooked in psychedelic trials 13 .
text.formatted: Its primary purpose is classified as supportive care; the primary endpoint is change in depression severity (MADRS) from baseline to 6 weeks after the second dosing session, and secondary outcomes include anxiety, demoralization, quality of life, and longer-term patient and family wellbeing, an endpoint the investigators have specifically noted is often overlooked in psychedelic trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13</ref> .

text.text: Results are not yet published; the project began in January 2024 and the trial opened to enrollment in 2025; it is registered as NCT06782724.

Its significance for palliative care extends beyond any single diagnosis: PsyPal is the first trial to test whether the effect sizes documented in cancer populations replicate across mechanistically distinct forms of terminal and progressive disease, and its lack of an upper age limit means it will, for the first time, generate prospective safety data for older patients within a structured research protocol rather than relying on the small, incidental numbers of older participants captured in prior psychedelic trials 4.
text.formatted: Its significance for palliative care extends beyond any single diagnosis: PsyPal is the first trial to test whether the effect sizes documented in cancer populations replicate across mechanistically distinct forms of terminal and progressive disease, and its lack of an upper age limit means it will, for the first time, generate prospective safety data for older patients within a structured research protocol rather than relying on the small, incidental numbers of older participants captured in prior psychedelic trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4</ref>.

text.text: A second, independent program is testing psilocybin specifically in ALS.
Investigators Drs.

Ambereen Mehta and Albert Garcia-Romeu at Johns Hopkins University have initiated a clinical trial examining the effects of psilocybin on mood, hopelessness, and quality of life in patients with ALS 14 .
text.formatted: Ambereen Mehta and Albert Garcia-Romeu at Johns Hopkins University have initiated a clinical trial examining the effects of psilocybin on mood, hopelessness, and quality of life in patients with ALS <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14</ref> .

text.text: ALS carries a uniformly poor prognosis and a high burden of hopelessness and existential distress with few effective pharmacological options, which the investigators cite as the rationale for the trial 14, 15 .
text.formatted: ALS carries a uniformly poor prognosis and a high burden of hopelessness and existential distress with few effective pharmacological options, which the investigators cite as the rationale for the trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">15</ref> .

text.text: Related pilot work using microdose psilocybin in palliative populations is also underway in Canada, led by palliative physician James Downar at Bruyère Health in Ottawa, testing whether low, non-hallucinogenic doses can reduce psychological distress in patients receiving palliative care without the intensity of a full-dose session 16 .
text.formatted: Related pilot work using microdose psilocybin in palliative populations is also underway in Canada, led by palliative physician James Downar at Bruyère Health in Ottawa, testing whether low, non-hallucinogenic doses can reduce psychological distress in patients receiving palliative care without the intensity of a full-dose session <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">16</ref> .

text.text: An open-label Phase I/II study has since found microdose psilocybin safe and feasible, with signals of benefit, in patients with advanced, incurable illness 17 , and a multi-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial began recruiting in January 2026 18 .
text.formatted: An open-label Phase I/II study has since found microdose psilocybin safe and feasible, with signals of benefit, in patients with advanced, incurable illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">17</ref> , and a multi-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial began recruiting in January 2026 <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">18</ref> .

text.text: Downar has been explicit that the aim of this work is not to substitute for medical assistance in dying but to give patients additional time that is more bearable, a framing directly relevant to the tension examined in Section 3.3 below 16.
text.formatted: Downar has been explicit that the aim of this work is not to substitute for medical assistance in dying but to give patients additional time that is more bearable, a framing directly relevant to the tension examined in Section 3.3 below <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">16</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, PsyPal and the Johns Hopkins ALS trial represent the first coordinated effort to move psilocybin research beyond oncology and into the broader population of patients palliative care actually serves.

Neither trial has yet reported results, and neither establishes psilocybin as an approved therapy for these indications; their significance for this review is that they are, for the first time, generating age-inclusive, diagnosis-diverse safety and efficacy data directly relevant to palliative practice, rather than requiring that practice extrapolate from oncology or from healthyvolunteer studies.
Evidence from regulated non-research settings offers a complementary, if less controlled, picture.

A prospective cohort of 2,363 adults using Oregon and Colorado's regulated psilocybin services found depression scores improved 49% and anxiety scores improved 51% at two weeks, with only 4% mild and 0.2% more serious adverse events recorded, although the authors are explicit that these are observational associations, not controlled trial results 19 (Figure 1).
text.formatted: A prospective cohort of 2,363 adults using Oregon and Colorado's regulated psilocybin services found depression scores improved 49% and anxiety scores improved 51% at two weeks, with only 4% mild and 0.2% more serious adverse events recorded, although the authors are explicit that these are observational associations, not controlled trial results <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">19</ref> (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: A separate, peerreviewed 346-person cohort through Oregon's program, followed to three months, found four serious adverse behavioral reactions (about 1% of participants), all in psychedelic-naive individuals with pre-existing symptoms of depression, anxiety and/or PTSD 20 .
text.formatted: A separate, peerreviewed 346-person cohort through Oregon's program, followed to three months, found four serious adverse behavioral reactions (about 1% of participants), all in psychedelic-naive individuals with pre-existing symptoms of depression, anxiety and/or PTSD <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">20</ref> .

text.text: Evidence is necessary but not sufficient for access.
Three barriers recur across the jurisdictions and populations reviewed here, and each bears directly on whether a palliative patient who might benefit from psilocybin-assisted therapy can obtain it.

Older adults and patients with the progressive, multi-morbid conditions typical of palliative care have historically been excluded from psychedelic trials, often without a stated rationale: a review of trials in four major medical journals found that 92.8% of studies with an upper age limit gave no explanation for the cut-off 5 , and only 1.4% of participants across 36 psilocybin trials were aged 65 or older 4 .
text.formatted: Older adults and patients with the progressive, multi-morbid conditions typical of palliative care have historically been excluded from psychedelic trials, often without a stated rationale: a review of trials in four major medical journals found that 92.8% of studies with an upper age limit gave no explanation for the cut-off <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">5</ref> , and only 1.4% of participants across 36 psilocybin trials were aged 65 or older <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4</ref> .

text.text: This creates what might be called evidentiary circularity: the absence of data on a population is then used to justify continuing to exclude it, a pattern visible in regulatory decisions such as Australia's 2026 interim scheduling review, which cited limited supporting evidence for psilocybin use in existential distress at end of life 23 .

text.text: PsyPal and the Hopkins ALS trial are notable precisely because they are structured to break this cycle rather than reproduce it.
Where legal access exists, it is often expensive.
In Australia, a course of pharmaceutical-grade psilocybin therapy for treatment-resistant depression costs approximately AUD 20,000 24.

text.text: This cost is driven less by the strength of the underlying clinical evidence than by the current regulatory framework a product is filed under: establishing a substance as a registered medicine requires GMP production and a full marketingauthorization pathway, while the same effect delivered outside that framework, as with the Netherlands' food-law-based sale of psilocybin-containing truffles, can be substantially cheaper, illustrating that systematic exclusion by cost is a policy choice rather than a scientific necessity.

Without parallel funding or subsidy mechanisms, removing systematic regulatory barriers to access risks simply replacing them with a wealth-based one, a concern directly relevant to palliative populations, who often face high care costs already.

Even the furthest-advanced medicines-pathway program illustrates how slow that route remains even as it nears completion: Compass Pathways' COMP360 met its primary endpoint in both pivotal Phase 3 trials for treatment-resistant depression by early 2026 28 , and 52-week open-label data reported in September 2026 showed sustained benefit through one year and no new safety signals, with the U.S. new drug application completed on November 9, 2026, under a Commissioner's National Priority Voucher targeting a one-to-two-month review 29 , and commercial launch anticipated in the first half of 2027, subject to FDA approval 30 ; no jurisdiction had completed marketing authorization for it at the time of writing.

text.text: The juxtaposition -slow or refused access to a potentially reversible intervention against rapid approval for an irreversible one -raises a direct question for palliative systems about whether current thresholds are internally coherent.

This sits within a broader pattern: a 2026 survey of 121 Canadian palliative care stakeholders found overall attitudes toward psilocybin-assisted therapy for existential distress were only 39% favorable, concealing a striking split in which 95% of physicians specifically reported favorable views; the barrier stakeholders identified as primary was a shortage of trained providers, not physician resistance, and 68% favored introducing the therapy earlier in a life-limiting illness rather than reserving it for the very end of life 1 .

text.text: The case for individualized eligibility rests on a narrower claim than that psilocybin is proven beneficial for palliative populations: that a patient who understands the disclosed risks, uncertainties, and limitations of a supervised psilocybin experience should be able to accept or decline it.
This should be subject to the same requirements of capacity, voluntariness, and clinical screening applied to other consequential decisions in serious illness care.

This argument does not depend on waiting for definitive trial results, because the population being asked to wait is frequently the same population least represented in the trials that would produce that evidence, and because for patients with a terminal or rapidly progressive diagnosis, time itself is a scarce resource that systematic exclusion spends without their consent.
Systematic exclusion by age or diagnosis replaces individualized clinical judgment with a blunt rule.

This is not a new tension in palliative care ethics, which already routinely balances patient autonomy against paternalistic caution in decisions with comparable stakes such as enrollment in early-phase trials.

Age-based exclusion specifically is difficult to justify on the evidence reviewed in Section 2: it is not that older or multi-morbid patients have been shown to tolerate psilocybin poorly, but that they have rarely been studied, and the two are not the same finding.

Where the evidence base does raise a genuine caution, it is cardiovascular and psychiatric risk assessed at the level of the individual patient, not chronological age or diagnostic category as such 21, 37.

text.text: Physician and public information gaps compound these barriers.

Decades of restrictive scheduling have kept psilocybin outside most medical curricula, and a 2024 survey of U.S. healthcare professionals found generally low objective knowledge of its benefit-risk ratio and uses, with physicians reporting less openness than nurses 38 .
text.formatted: Decades of restrictive scheduling have kept psilocybin outside most medical curricula, and a 2024 survey of U.S. healthcare professionals found generally low objective knowledge of its benefit-risk ratio and uses, with physicians reporting less openness than nurses <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">38</ref> .

text.text: For palliative care specifically, closing this gap is a precondition for the kind of individualized assessment this section argues for: clinicians cannot assess a treatment option they have not been trained to discuss.

This concern about burden on services and providers is real, particularly given the workforce shortage identified in the Canadian survey above 1 , but it is an argument for investment in training and capacity, not for withholding the option from patients who might benefit.
Jurisdictions currently take markedly different approaches to eligibility.
Oregon's regulated psilocybin services, established under Measure 109, require individualized preparation and screening by licensed facilitators rather than an upper-age rule 39 .
text.formatted: Oregon's regulated psilocybin services, established under Measure 109, require individualized preparation and screening by licensed facilitators rather than an upper-age rule <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">39</ref> .

text.text: The Netherlands permits psilocybin-containing truffles under food law, available to any adult without individualized clinical screening, an approach that lowers cost and removes age-based barriers entirely.

Narrower medical-necessity pathways, including Canada's Special Access Program discussed above, Australia's authorized-prescriber framework, and comparable routes in Germany, Switzerland, and the Czech Republic, sit between these poles, generally permitting access case-by-case but at substantial cost and with variable waiting times.

New Mexico's Medical Psilocybin Act (2025) is notable for listing end-of-life care among its qualifying conditions alongside treatment-resistant depression, PTSD, and substance use disorders, with first patients targeted by December 2026 40 ; it shows that a diagnosis-gated framework can recognize palliative need directly rather than requiring a qualifying psychiatric diagnosis.

text.text: Several Asian jurisdictions illustrate the restrictive end of this range and are worth naming alongside the European and North American frameworks discussed above.

South Korea classifies psilocybin as a controlled psychotropic substance requiring regulatory approval even for trace-amount academic research and, unusually, asserts extraterritorial jurisdiction over its own citizens, so that a Korean national who used psilocybin lawfully in a permissive jurisdiction can still be prosecuted at home 42, 43, 44 .

These restrictive regulatory frameworks matter for palliative care specifically because they foreclose not only patient access but the clinical research needed to eventually inform it, reinforcing the evidentiary circularity described in Section 3.1.

This patchwork matters for palliative populations specifically because time-limited prognoses make waiting times and administrative delays a clinically meaningful barrier in a way they are not for most other patient groups.
A regulatory framework that is workable in principle can still fail a patient with a terminal diagnosis if it takes eleven months to resolve, as in the Canadian case above.

Furthermore, without parallel public funding, jurisdictions that relax systematic exclusions risk making individualized access available mainly to patients who can pay privately, replacing one barrier with another.

Finally, the scientific case for individualized, diagnosis-inclusive access is beginning to be made in jurisdictions with far more restrictive general drug policy, including small but methodologically serious research programs now underway in East Asia (to date, chiefly in Japan) despite considerable legal and professional risk to the investigators involved 46, 49 .

text.text: Their existence suggests that the gap between documented palliative need and permitted access is not a fixed cultural preference but a policy choice subject to revision as evidence accumulates, the same conclusion this article reaches for the jurisdictions discussed above.
Four findings translate directly into recommendations for palliative care systems and policymakers.
Move from systematic to individualized eligibility.

Where psilocybin-assisted therapy is legally available, eligibility criteria should assess cardiovascular status, psychiatric history, and decision-making capacity in each patient rather than applying blanket age or diagnostic exclusions not supported by the evidence reviewed in Section 2.

Funders and trial sponsors should require minimum representation of older adults and patients with the progressive, multi-morbid conditions typical of palliative populations, building on the precedent PsyPal and the Hopkins ALS trial have already set, so that age-specific and diagnosis-specific evidence continues to accumulate rather than stalling once these two programs report.
Pair any expansion of access with funding mechanisms.

Jurisdictions considering broader psilocybin-assisted therapy access should build in public funding, subsidy, or insurance coverage from the outset, so that reduced systematic exclusion does not simply shift the barrier from age or diagnosis to ability to pay.

Closing the documented gap in clinician knowledge of psilocybin's risks and uses is a precondition for the individualized clinical assessment this article recommends, and should be incorporated into palliative care training specifically, given the workforce shortage identified as the primary barrier in the Canadian stakeholder survey 1.

text.text: Systematic age-or diagnosis-based exclusion from psilocybin-assisted therapy is not supported by the evidence currently available and should, where access is legally permitted, be replaced by individualized assessment of relevant physical, psychiatric, and capacity-related risk factors.

Clinicians should distinguish informed-consent capacity, which most palliative patients retain, from proof of medical benefit, which remains under active investigation in trials such as PsyPal and the Hopkins ALS study.

The evidence base for psilocybin-assisted therapy in serious and life-limiting illness is shifting quickly, from a foundation built almost entirely on oncology and healthy-volunteer studies toward trials, pioneered by the PsyPal project and the Johns Hopkins ALS program, designed specifically for the diagnostically diverse, often older population palliative care actually serves.
Neither program has yet reported results, and this article does not argue that psilocybin can be treated as an established medicine for existential distress in serious illness.

It argues for a narrower yet more immediate principle: where legal access already exists, eligibility should be determined by individualized clinical assessment of capacity, risk, and voluntariness (personal autonomy) rather than by systematic exclusions, including age-based cut-offs, that the evidence reviewed here does not support.

The barriers documented in this review -evidentiary circularity, cost, regulatory fragmentation, and gaps in clinician training -are policy choices, not scientific necessities, and each is addressable independent of how the ongoing trials resolve.

As PsyPal, the Hopkins ALS trial, and comparable programs report their results over the coming years, palliative care systems have an opportunity to build eligibility frameworks now that will not need to be rebuilt once that evidence arrives.
